subject: NeuraHealth pilot: GPU allocation, tokens/sec fit, and tail-latency safety margin
messages: From: Irene Choi To: Ben Carter , Vanessa Ortiz Date: Tue, 22 Jun 2027 09:12:00 -0700 Subject: Internal: NeuraHealth pilot sizing notes (tokens/sec + tail latency) Ben/Vanessa — Quick read-ahead before we send the draft sizing to Alicia at NeuraHealth. Key asks from the product/infra review: they want a committed Dedicated pool for a 90-day pilot with an SLO of 95% requests <= 300ms tail for short prompts (~128 tokens) and a soft SLO for longer generation (~1024 tokens) targeting 1.2s 95th. They expect bursty activity aligned to clinician hours: 09:00-17:00 PT with a 3x peak multiplier. My baseline numbers from our bench: on A100-80GB (fp16) the 30B model (quantized) gives ~450 tokens/sec steady per GPU at seq_len=1024 with effective continuous batching (batch=8). For short prompts (128 tokens) under low context reuse we get ~1100 tokens/sec per GPU. Tail-latency overhead (95th) grows ~1.6x vs median under realistic concurrency and KV cache misses. Proposed conservative build for pilot (to include headroom for burst and routing fallbacks): - Pilot target peak TPS (tokens/sec) requirement: estimate 900k tokens/sec peak across fleet (derived from their forecasted QPS x median token output). - Recommended committed GPUs: 48 x A100-80GB (reserved) -> nominal steady capacity ~21.6M tokens/sec aggregate (using an operational factor 0.8), but effective per-deal allocation after multi-tenancy and routing reserves = 0.04 of fleet for pilot. This translates to comfortable headroom for 3x peaks and 2x safety. But we should translate to SLO fit math in the note we send to procurement, with simple bullets and a one-sheet attachment (spreadsheet with per-GPU tokens/sec lines, assumptions, and burst model). Action items for our outbound: Ben to confirm pricing for a 48-GPU reserved slab + burst lanes; Vanessa to draft the SLO language (95th tail, rolling 1h window, fallback to smaller-gen model). I'll attach the quick calc and ship to Alicia. Irene Director, Solutions Engineering Redwood Inference Attachment: neurahealth_draft_sizing.xlsx (spreadsheet stub) From: Irene Choi To: Alicia Ramirez Cc: procurement@neurahealth.ai, Ben Carter , Vanessa Ortiz Date: Tue, 22 Jun 2027 11:05:00 -0700 Subject: NeuraHealth pilot: Dedicated GPU allocation & SLO proposal Hi Alicia — Thanks again for the productive call earlier. Per our discussion, attached is a concise sizing proposal for the 90-day pilot that maps your projected traffic profile into dedicated GPU allocation and shows headroom for bursts and latency safety. High-level summary below; see the attached spreadsheet for line-by-line math. Summary of assumptions (short): - Model variant: rwd-30b-quant (recommended for clinical summarization workflows) - Prompt profile: 60% short (<=128 tokens), 40% long (~1024 tokens produced) - Clinician-hours burst multiplier: 3x peak during 09:00-17:00 PT - Target SLOs: short prompts 95th <= 300ms; long generations 95th <= 1.2s Sizing conclusion (pilot): - Recommended committed slab: 24 reserved GPUs (A100-80GB equiv) + 8 burst-capacity GPUs on-demand. - Expected steady tokens/sec served by reserved slab: ~9.6M tokens/sec (operational factor applied). - Burst headroom: on-demand lanes provide an extra ~3.2M tokens/sec during peak windows; combined gives >2.5x buffer to estimated peak. - Tail-latency margin: we budget an extra 50% capacity to account for KV cache churn and worst-case concurrency spikes (this keeps 95th latency under targets in our sims). Next steps I propose: 1) Procurement review: if the slab count looks right, Ben will circulate term pricing and a DocuSign for the pilot commit. 2) Technical kickoff: schedule a 60-min deployment plan with your infra team; we'll include routing and KV-cache warmup steps to reduce early tail spikes. 3) SLA draft: Vanessa will propose the 95th-window definitions and fallback model (smaller model variant + rate limiting) — we suggest a canary rollback policy if 95th latency exceeds objective for >30m contiguous windows. I've attached the spreadsheet (neurahealth_draft_sizing.xlsx) and a two-pager on tail-latency considerations (nh-sla-tail-latency-walkthrough.pdf). Would you be available Thursday 23rd 10:00 PT for the technical kickoff? Thanks, Irene Choi Director, Solutions Engineering | Redwood Inference Attachment: neurahealth_draft_sizing.xlsx, nh-sla-tail-latency-walkthrough.pdf From: Alicia Ramirez To: Irene Choi Cc: procurement@neurahealth.ai Date: Tue, 22 Jun 2027 15:44:00 -0700 Subject: Re: NeuraHealth pilot: Dedicated GPU allocation & SLO proposal Irene — Thanks, this is helpful and far more concrete than we expected. A few quick clarifying questions from our engineering lead: 1) Your per-GPU tokens/sec numbers look optimistic compared to our internal microbenchmarks for rwd-30b-quant at seq=1024 — we get ~380 tokens/sec under similar batching; can you share the batch sizes and concurrency assumptions used? 2) For the 95th tail margin, can you show the simulation that drove the 50% headroom number? We need to present that to our compliance lead. 3) Procurement: on the reserved slab sizing — can we pilot with 18 reserved + 6 burst instead of 24 + 8? That would materially reduce cash outlay and still might be workable if latency fallbacks are enabled early. Thursday 23rd 10:00 PT works for the kickoff. Please include someone from your SRE team to walk through KV cache warmup and routing. Best, Alicia Ramirez Head of Integrations NeuraHealth From: Ben Carter To: Alicia Ramirez , Irene Choi Cc: Vanessa Ortiz , procurement@neurahealth.ai Date: Wed, 23 Jun 2027 11:03:00 -0700 Subject: Re: NeuraHealth pilot: Dedicated GPU allocation & SLO proposal Alicia — Thanks for the quick review and excellent questions. Short answers, and we'll show the sims in tomorrow's kickoff. 1) Bench assumptions: our spreadsheet line items use an operational batching profile: typical batch size=6 (avg), concurrency=18 across slab during peak windows, with prefix/KV caching for repeated patient-context tokens. The 450 tokens/sec per GPU figure in Irene's note is a median-of-run benchmark using our runtime with continuous batching and kernel-level optimizations; that maps to ~380 tokens/sec in your microbench when you account for cold KV cache and lower effective batching. We'll include both lines in the sheet so you can compare apples-to-apples. 2) Tail-latency sim: we ran a synthetic trace with the customer's expected traffic shape (3x burst with 60% short/40% long), injected 20% cache-miss events, and modeled request queuing using a 95th-percentile service-time distribution derived from our telemetry. The 50% headroom is the conservative safety factor to keep simulated 95th under the stated SLO across plausible worst-case routing failures. We'll export the sim summary into the Google Drive doc for your compliance team (link above). 3) Pilot slab compromise: 18 reserved + 6 burst is a reasonable starting point if we (a) enable fallback to rwd-7b-quant for non-critical long-run requests, and (b) pre-warm KV caches during the first 30 minutes of clinician hours. Operationally we'd recommend a canary 48-hour ramp where we monitor 95th latency closely and be prepared to spin additional burst capacity. Pricing-wise, Ben will put both term options in the DocuSign (18+6 and 24+8) — procurement can pick. See you Thursday 10:00 PT — adding SRE (Josef Park) to the invite. Regards, Ben Carter Principal Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference Attachment: none
